deep.reconstruction:
Page 27 contains no derivation. It is a methodological note followed by the first line of a new proof.

(A) Heuristic note. Hilbert lists reasons why, despite much brooding, one fails to find the solution of a mathematical question.
1) One aims at too much and sets the goal too far ('the time is not yet ripe', as people say). Long preparatory work is needed, after which the solution falls out like a ripe fruit.
2) The number of collected individual phenomena ('Einzelerscheinungen') is still too small. Enlarge the collection by pushing out in all directions. The missing phenomena often lie in apparently quite different fields, and the solution then often reveals a connection between those fields.
3) Simpler related questions believed to be completely settled have not actually been worked through and understood to their completion. So first present all simpler related problems with known solution in such a way that everything specific to them recedes as far as possible. The theory then usually becomes capable of generalisation.

(B) Start of a proof, continued on the next page. Claim: the Galois field generated by all conjugate fields of an equation with symmetric Galois group contains no roots of unity except possibly i.

The argument on the next page, in modern terms:
- Let K be the splitting field of an irreducible f of degree n over Q with Gal(K/Q) = S_n.
- If K contains a root of unity zeta, then Q(zeta) is an abelian subextension. So some rational function phi of the roots has a power phi^k that is symmetric, i.e. rational.
- Hilbert argues that phi must be the alternating function prod(alpha_i - alpha_j) and k = 2. A transposition (alpha beta) fixes phi^k, so it can only multiply phi by a factor whose k-th power is 1; he asserts that factor is -1, hence (alpha - beta) divides phi, and so on.
- In modern language: the commutator subgroup of S_n is A_n and S_n/A_n has order 2. So the only abelian subfield of K is Q(sqrt(D)), D the discriminant. Any root of unity in K must therefore lie in a field of degree at most 2.
errors: The conclusion begun at the foot of this page and finished on the next page is too strong as stated. The argument correctly shows that roots of unity in K must lie in the unique quadratic subfield Q(sqrt(D)). That field can be Q(sqrt(-3)) as well as Q(i). Counterexample: x^3 - 2 has Galois group S_3, discriminant -108 = -3*6^2, and its splitting field contains the primitive cube root of unity (-1+sqrt(-3))/2. So 'except possibly i' should read 'except possibly i or primitive 3rd/6th roots of unity (besides -1)'.

On the next page, the step 'the base can only change by the factor -1' is asserted rather than proved. One needs that a transposition, an element of order 2, multiplies phi by a root of unity of order dividing 2, and the choice of the factor needs justification.

results.what: Heuristic maxims on why mathematical problems resist solution: premature goals, too few collected special cases, and simpler related problems not fully understood, to be recast so that their special features recede and they become generalisable.
results.modern_name: Mathematical heuristics; specialisation and generalisation (cf. the 1900 Paris problems address)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert himself expresses similar views publicly in 'Mathematische Probleme' (1900); cf. later Pólya, 'How to Solve It' (1945)

results.what: The splitting field of an equation with full symmetric group contains only roots of unity lying in its unique quadratic subfield (stated by Hilbert as 'none except possibly i').
results.modern_name: Maximal abelian subextension of an S_n-extension is Q(sqrt(disc)), since the commutator subgroup of S_n is A_n
results.usually_credited_to: Classical Galois theory (Galois, Jordan, Kronecker; 19th century)

deep.surprise_reason: The heuristic maxims are an early private formulation of ideas Hilbert later stated in his 1900 problems lecture. They are of some biographical interest, but this kind of material from the Hilbert notebooks is known to historians (Rowe, Corry). The Galois-theory fragment is routine and slightly misstated.

checkable.asserts: The discriminant of x^3-2 is -108 = -3*36, so sqrt(D) generates Q(sqrt(-3)). This is a counterexample to 'only i'.
x^3-2 splits completely over Q(2^(1/3), sqrt(-3)), so its S_3 splitting field contains sqrt(-3) and hence cube roots of unity.

checkable.sympy: from sympy.combinatorics import SymmetricGroup; G=SymmetricGroup(4); G.order()//G.derived_subgroup().order() == 2
checkable.asserts: The abelianisation of S_n (here n=4) has order 2, so there is a unique abelian (quadratic) subextension.
(-1+sqrt(-3))/2 is a primitive cube root of unity lying in Q(sqrt(-3)).
